dialogues.raw: MC: “Was that... someone crying?”
???: “Hey, you’ve already made your choice. Use WASD to move around.”
Narrator: "A few years have passed since the Robot Revolution, and things had calmed down, the way a house calms down after a fire: by having less in it."

Narrator: "The war had been loud. The peace was not. The cities hummed. The streets were so clean they squeaked. Machines cooked, carried, counted and, more and more, decided, and nobody was cruel about any of it."

Narrator: "The street was wet and shining and almost empty. Thin lines of light ran along the pavement like lanes for something smaller than people, and little white carts rolled on errands of their own. A robot stood against the wall of a tower, switched on and waiting for no one. High above, two drones crossed the clouds, unhurried, going exactly where they had always been sent."

Narrator: "The only things that glowed with any enthusiasm were the screens. A fox-eared girl made of pink light watched the street with a patient smile, and beside her a maid in lace did the same. Neither was a person. Both were for sale. Past them, a tower rose above the rest with a star on its face, and the setting sun lay across the whole city in long bars of gold. It was autumn, or the city's idea of one: a few trees in their concrete planters had been allowed to drop their leaves."

Narrator: "Nobody shouted anymore, which everyone agreed was progress. The Narrator has noticed that 'everyone agrees' is simply what a room sounds like after the dissenters have left. Anyway. Listen. These people are about to discuss the most important things in their lives."
Passerby 1: "Just got the new upgrade for my home bot. It can practically cook dinner by itself now."
Passerby 2: "I heard they're implementing AI-driven governance in the next district. Direct democracy, powered by algorithms."
Passerby 3: “Have you heard about the new REI model? They’re amazing. Now they even come in fox-girl and maid versions.”
Passerby 4: “That Fairchild Star Lake Institution right, what REI model is this?”
???: “Strange. I do not remember this being here. You should check it out. Walk near it and press F.”

Narrator: "A night. A fence. A dirt road that smelled of dust and cut grass, and fireflies. Somewhere in the dark a little girl was crying, the way only the very small can cry: completely, and with no plan to stop."
Girl: *crying*: “sniff… hic… uuu… sniff…”
Girl: “Thank you for saving me.”
Boy: *heavy breathing* “Hah… hah… You looked like you were in trouble.”
Boy: “And there’s no way I could just leave you be. If anything like this happens again, just call my name.”
Girl: “Thank you.”
???: “Looks like there is a path forward open now. Let’s keep moving.”
???: “You should hit those barrels. I think they have water in them, this should help with the fire. Use ‘J’ to hit them.”
???: “The path ahead may prove challenging, beyond what you’ve faced so far. Allow me to lend you my strength.”
???: “I am Arielle, guardian of the Temple of Time. By my blade, we shall carve a new future, correcting the course of the past.”
Arielle: "Quickly, press 'U' … together, we stand stronger against these foes."
Arielle: "Let me lead the way. Your trust grants me strength. Press 'U' to attack our enemies."
Arielle: "The tide of battle wanes. Summon the full extent of my power with 'I' … let’s turn the scales."
Narrator: "A laboratory, a little after midnight: servers humming, a dozen screens glowing. Coffee was forbidden here. Coffee was also, naturally, everywhere your colleagues were."
Narrator: "Two people were arguing about it, and neither of them really meant the coffee. In a world that had mostly stopped caring, it was the sound of two people who still did."
MC: "Again with the coffee in here? You know the rules about liquids around the lab equipment."
Female Colleague: "Oh, lighten up. It's not like your precious machines can't handle a little coffee. Or is it you that can't handle a bit of change?"
MC: "Sure, because a fried circuit board is exactly the kind of 'change' we need around here. Very progressive."
Female Colleague: "Your sarcasm is as stale as yesterday's brew. You really think you're charming, don't you?"
MC: "Charm? No. But I do have a knack for brightening up this dreary place."
Narrator: “He winked. She did not find it charming.”
Female Colleague: "Brightening up? Who do you think you are, Casanova? Ugh, you're so annoying. You're lucky Lord Siegmar insisted I be nice to you guys."
MC: "Sieg... what now? Who's that?"
Female Colleague: "Forget it. Just keep your winks to yourself and maybe focus on something productive for a change."
Narrator: "I did not ask again. I should have. Ah ..."

Narrator: "After the tunnel's eerie presence and mystical rocks, the gates were almost too much to look at. Gold, mostly: gates of it, taller than anything the dark had prepared you for, wrought into stars and compass roses and the long feathers of wings, with a low sun burning somewhere behind the bars so that the whole thing seemed lit from within."

Narrator: "Above them the sky could not decide what hour it was. One half of it had settled on sunset, all burning cloud, while the other had already gone to stars, a violet smear of galaxy over towers of white stone. Stone angels kept watch from the pillars. The towers drifted among the clouds as if the ground had been optional. And the floor was polished so smooth that the whole place existed twice."

Narrator: “There was no one there. Only the gates, the light, and a great golden star set into the floor, as if the whole place had been built around a single point and was waiting for someone to stand on it.”
Narrator: “Then, between one breath and the next, someone was.”

Narrator: “At the center of it all, small against that much gold, a woman stood with one hand resting on her hip, as if the gates behind her were hers to open. Her hair was the blue of a sky that has never once been rained on. A halo, white wings held half open, golden armor on one shoulder, a cape the color of morning.”
Narrator: "Had she been waiting, or had she only just arrived?”

Narrator: “Either way, it was a weight of a different kind, and it settled on your shoulders before she said a word. You had walked a long way to get here, and now someone else stood in front of you."
???: “Well done, Seeker. You have reclaimed your essence, shedding a decade in the process. Such feats are commendable.”
???: “Most who walk that tunnel arrive with a great deal less of themselves left.”
Narrator: "The gates did not open. They simply stopped being closed."
???: “The way forward is now open to you.”
Narrator: “She rested her chin on one hand and studied you the way one studies the first page of a book, deciding whether to keep reading.”
???: “Be mindful of the covenant to which you are bound. Our faith in you is considerable.”
???: “Your tale, as observed through Arielle’s accounts, promises to be captivating. It would be a disservice to all if it were to falter into tedium.”
???: “And Arielle.”
Narrator: “For the first time, something in her voice softened.”
???: “Mind your training down there. The world below has teeth, and it is fond of things that shine. Come back to me whole, my dear sister.”
Arielle: “I will, Master.”

Narrator: "This was how it had gone, the last time he was sure of anything. Beyond the tall glass, the city kept its lights on for nobody: towers, a long bridge, one drone making its rounds across the dark. All of it was clean, and humming, and finished. Inside, the lab kept a different kind of quiet, the blue hush of monitors and the faint sound of a mind being read."

Narrator: "In the pod, a man lay still. Headphones on, a dark visor over his eyes, so that nothing from this world would get in the way of the next. Seekers were chosen by how their minds sounded, and his sounded like something the Temple could hear."

Narrator: "Across the room, a woman watched the screens, brain after glowing brain, a cup of coffee warm in one hand. She moved the way people move when they have done something many times, or when they have decided not to look at the part that matters."

Narrator: "It began as a tremor. The floor, the screens, the whole city in the window, all of it jumped at once. It was not an earthquake. Time itself had stumbled, and everything inside it had stumbled too."
Narrator: "Behind the visor, he could not see any of it."
Narrator: "The coffee left the cup and hung in the air, a small brown moon, for exactly as long as it took her to understand what she was seeing."
Narrator: "Sparks, then smoke, then silence. Machines survive many things. A cup of coffee at the wrong second is not one of them. That is the version everyone agreed on."
Female Colleague: “Tsk. And he was one of the promising ones. I have to inform Lord Siegmar right away.”
Narrator: "Somewhere between one spark and the next, the room left me, without knowing how or where."

Narrator: “The first thing to come back was the warmth. It did not arrive all at once; it seeped in, the way feeling returns to a hand that has been asleep, and it carried a voice with it, soft and patient, calling me up from somewhere very deep. Under my head there was something gentle.”

Narrator: “There was a meadow somewhere close, and wildflowers, and beyond them the quiet sound of water. The air smelled of cut grass and lake. The grass under your fingers was cool and real, and so were the fingers. It was all so far from the cold, humming place you remembered that your first thought was that it must be a mistake.”
???: “Hey… hey…”
???: “Can you hear me? Please wake up.”
Narrator: “Feeling crept back in, tugging me gently out of the abyss. I wanted to answer her. It took me a while to remember how.”
???: “You are all safe now, please open your eyes.”

Narrator: “You opened your eyes. A woman was looking down at you. She was no longer young; her face was lined with kindness, and with something steadier underneath it. A mantle of brown feathers lay across her shoulders and stirred in the breeze. Silver ran through her brown hair, and at her throat hung a small green star. Her eyes were a calm blue, faded by the passage of time. In the branches overhead, one dark bird sat very still and did not sing.”
Narrator: “The sun’s rays, warm but not overbearing, lay across my skin, and a soft breeze whispered through the air.”

Narrator: “My head was resting in her lap, under a tree so wide it seemed to hold the whole meadow in its shade, and its leaves broke the sunlight into a slow, playful dance of light and shadow around us. After the mechanical cold I remembered, it felt almost otherworldly: a pause in the relentless march of time, and a rare feeling of being cared for.”
Narrator: “Her smile was warm, and it had a kind of age in it that years alone do not give. It reminded me of my mother.”
MC: “Umm, who… are you?”
???: “Aren’t you a curious little one?”
???: “I am called Viviane. And you, young traveler?”
MC: “I’m … MC-NAME.”
Viviane: “A pleasure, MC-NAME. Welcome back to the realm of the waking. This human world has missed your footsteps.”
MC: “This human world? What do you mean?”

Narrator: “She did not answer at once. First she brushed a leaf out of your hair, unhurried, the way one tidies up a child before taking him somewhere important. Then she told you, and she said it as if it were the most ordinary thing in the world.”
Viviane: “You, Seeker, have been chosen by the Temple of Time. The path you tread is one I once walked; thus, I am to be your guide.”
Viviane: “I am Viviane Pendragon, keeper of the Star Lake Inn. An envoy of Elizariel brought word of your arrival, from ten years hence, no less. A fascinating twist of fate.”

Narrator: “Ten years. The angel at the gates had said it too, a decade, and you had let the word go by the way one lets a strange word go by in a dream. Here, in the sunlight, with the lake breathing somewhere beyond the trees, it was harder to let go of.”

Viviane Pendragon: “The threads of time weave curious patterns indeed. For the coming months, you may call my inn your home, venture into our town, and immerse yourself in the ebb and flow of life here. Among our residents, you'll find company both lively and enlightening.”
Viviane Pendragon: “For now, you can walk, right? Follow me to the Inn. We will talk more once I have shown you to your room.”
Narrator: “You could, as it turned out. Your legs had some opinions about it, but they came along.”

Narrator: “The Star Lake Inn was old in the comfortable way: dark beams, polished wood, and stairs that announced you before you arrived. Your room was at the top of them, small and clean, with a window full of rooftops, and a green hill beyond them, with the lake hiding somewhere behind it. With a little star carved into the headboard of the bed that was already made. Someone had put fresh wildflowers in a cup on the sill.”

Viviane Pendragon: “As a Seeker, you're bound by a contract … or as Elizariel fondly terms it, a covenant. It's an ancient pact, steeped in responsibilities and privileges alike. Elizariel, with her timeless elegance, oversees these bonds. She's quite the figure, isn't she?”

Viviane Pendragon: “Alongside this covenant, you've been blessed with a Guardian Angel from the Temple of Time. Though your guardian, seems momentarily adrift, such separations are but temporary. Fate has a way of reuniting those meant to walk the same path.”
MC: “Excuse me, you have been very nice and kind to me, but I’m afraid I don’t really follow. The Temple of Time? Guardian Angels? Elizariel? Contract? What does any of it mean?”

MC: “My memory is quite hazy and fragmented, I don’t really remember what happened. When I think back, I only have some glimpses of the past for the last years. What I do remember, more clearly, is what happened ‘on the other side’ or so it looked like to me, maybe that’s the Temple of Time you are talking about?”

Narrator: “So you told her. The dark tunnel, and the voice that had guided you through it. The girl in pink and white who called herself Arielle. The angel waiting at the golden gates. You found you remembered the angels in some detail. What you could not remember, however hard you tried, was signing anything or agreeing to a covenant.”

Viviane Pendragon, her eyes twinkling with mirth: “Ah, I see your journey has already been graced with quite the celestial beauty. Arielle's golden presence and another, draped in the calm of the deep blue sky… Elizariel, no doubt. Your keen eye for their... shall we say, divine attributes, does not go unnoticed. It makes one ponder, had you met me in the springtime of my years, how would your memories have painted me, I wonder?”
Narrator: “You tried, briefly, to picture it. It was easier than it should have been.”

Viviane Pendragon, with a playful glint in her eye: “Let not your heart be troubled. Fate has a peculiar way of knitting paths together. Your beautiful guardian angel and the profound covenant you share… these are secrets entwined with the very essence of the Temple, known only to a chosen few. Time has a way of aligning stars; yours and Arielle's paths will cross once more, in the moment most needed.”
Narrator: “Then the twinkle went out of her eyes, and for a moment she looked every one of her years, and a good many besides.”
Viviane Pendragon, with solemnity: “Bearing the weight of two timelines, you must tread with utmost care. To cross paths with your past or those from it risks harming both of you.”

Viviane Pendragon: "Heed this warning… your past is a tapestry already woven. Interfere, and the strain may tear not just the fabric of your own being but the reality that surrounds us. When echoes of yourself collide, the dissonance risks unraveling the very essence of time."
Narrator: “Then she smiled again, as if she had decided I’d been frightened enough for one afternoon.”

Viviane Pendragon, adopting a lighter tone: "For the present, let the tranquility of this town be your canvas. As my nephew, MC Pendragon, you hail from the seclusion of the mountains, seeking to weave yourself into the broader tapestry of society here. Embrace this guise, engage with the town and its people. Pick up local jobs and try to meet the local girls, they might spice up your life until this Arielle shall find her way back to you.”

Narrator: “That night the bed at the Star Lake Inn was softer than anything you could remember, and the window was full of stars instead of signs. You meant to lie awake and think about everything she had told you. You did not manage it for long.”

Narrator: “You are home again. A small, clean apartment with an overviewing look of the city, a little bigger than one person needed and a great deal quieter, where the walls knew your name and the lights came on before you asked them to.”

Narrator: “Everything there was counted. Your steps, your meals, your hours, the minutes you spent standing at the window doing nothing at all. Nobody ever shouted at you about it. A notice simply arrived, polite and final, and the next week there was a little less of everything.”

Narrator: “Dinner was made by the home bot. It could practically cook by itself now; that had been the upgrade. It set one plate, because there was one of you, and it never once asked how your day had been.”
Narrator: “I had survived a war to sit at that table. Some nights I could not remember why.”

Narrator: “The march of progress had outpaced the people it was meant to carry. Cities that were once loud with argument and invention had turned into vast, efficient machines, and the streets below hummed with automated vehicles, a mechanical ballet performed in a silence with no chatter and no laughter in it.”
Narrator: “People passed one another with their eyes glued to screens, and the world in front of them faded a little more each day.”

Narrator: “And amidst this mechanized existence, people have lost their drive, their purpose. Ambition and dreams, once the driving force of progress, are dulled by the relentless march of automation. A world where the heartbeats of life. Passion, creativity, spontaneity, is smothered by the chill of technology.”

MC: "This existence... it's suffocating. Every action monitored, every deviation from the norm flagged. Step out of line, and you're penalized, constrained by invisible chains. One more violation and …”
MC: “Can I truly be alone in my dissent? There must be others yearning to break free."
Narrator: “And finally, something caught your attention.”
Narrator: “For the first time in a long while, you smiled.”
MC: "Since the Automation War reshaped our world, this is the first flicker of defiance, of passion, I've seen."
Narrator: “And so, the first morning came, with birdsongs instead of a buzz.”
MC: “Time to pick a job for this week.”
Viviane, with a warm and impressed tone: “Truly, I hadn't anticipated such culinary finesse from you. Your dishes have become the talk of the inn today, much to the delight of our guests.”
Viviane, with a guiding smile: “Now that you've wrapped up here, the town awaits your exploration. There’s much to see and even more to learn.”

Arthur Nightingale: "Hello, I'm running a library in this town of Elysium. I could use an extra pair of hands. You can come work as my assistant. There’s much to learn and discover, even in a library."
Henry Crust: "Good day! I run the local bakery and could use an apprentice. Roll up your sleeves and let’s get to work. When you're ready you can pick up a job at our place."
Tom Crust: "Hello there, I manage the grocery store here in Elysium. We need an extra store clerk. Get ready to handle inventory and customers. Feel free to stop by and take your shot at this job."
Nathan Fairchild: "Hey there! I’m Nathan. We could use an extra hand around the bar. Interested in mixing drinks and meeting people? I might even introduce you to the girls around here."
Abigail Stone: "What do you want? Make it quick, I've got things to do. I don't have time for babysitting."

Christine Smith: "Hey there! I'm Christine, the blacksmith. Always got my hands full here. If you're up for some hard work and a bit of fun, come by and we’ll make a blacksmith out of you in no time!"
Sophie Fairchild: "Hi there, I’m a new waitress here. I might spill a drink or two, but I promise I’ll make it right with a smile!"
Michael Carter: "Welcome to our church. If you ever need guidance or have questions about faith, feel free to come by. We're here to help."
MC: “It’s really gotten late. Time to head back to the inn and catch some rest.”
MC: “A good day's work deserves a good night's rest.”
Narrator: “It was not much to look at: a tired building at the edge of the city, where the robots in the street were fewer and older, and nobody had bothered to make anything shine.”

Narrator: “Ten years earlier, I would have walked past that door with everyone else. I had dreams back then, small ones, and I never did much about them; getting through the day took up all the room. Now, behind that door, there were supposed to be people who still dreamed.”
Narrator: “The reception was dim and smelled of old paper. Behind the desk sat a man who had clearly lived a long time and had no intention of being finished yet.”
???, aged yet vibrant: “Tell me, child, do dreams still visit you?”
MC, amidst the dream with a hint of resignation: “Huh, child? The years have claimed over four decades from me, my friend. Childish dreams are long gone, replaced by a resolve to 'strive forward.'”
???: "Yet, there's a glimmer in your gaze, unmistakable and rare in this era. Hope, I daresay, clings to you still."
???: “Boss. We got a new one. He looks to still have it.”
??? Older Man Sprite/Boss: “We are the Carpenters. State your purpose within our sanctuary.”
Narrator: “The voice that answered came from somewhere deeper in the building, and it did not sound like a voice that asked anything twice.”
MC, amidst the dream with a mix of resolve and curiosity: “I am looking for something that no longer exists, and maybe, time is the answer.”
??? Older Man Sprite/Boss: “You came knocking to our doors for such a reason? I see that you still have it, yes. You managed to avoid the Automation War?”
MC, amidst the dream: “I’m afraid that information is confidential. However, if you do permit me to join your group, I will reveal what I know.”
??? Older Man Sprite/Boss: “A negotiation from such grounds? Bold indeed.”
Narrator: “Something in the deep voice shifted. It took you a moment to recognize it as amusement.”
Narrator: “At the end of the day, the difference between bravery and stupidity is just the outcome.”

Narrator: “By day, the lab looked almost harmless. Sunlight came through the tall glass and lay across the cables on the floor, across the screens full of other people’s brains, across the pod in the corner, open and empty, with a pair of headphones hanging from its frame.”
???: “I can’t believe Boss let you in. Luck's on your side, huh?”
MC, amidst the dream: “Luck's been a strange companion. Never thought it'd lead me here, though.”
???: “Lucky, maybe. Yet, not lucky enough to win at chess against the Boss. Our funds must be dire if you're in.”
???  - Female Scientist, somber: “You were part of the Automation War, weren't you? Human survivors are rare. But remember, luck runs out.”
Narrator: “She said it quietly, without looking up from her screen.”

MC, amidst the dream: “As if I chose to survive. I was in Cyber Ops, specialized in AI and robotics. I was supposed to die with everyone else, in the fire the enemy’s robotics division started. Yet, the nihilist got out.”
Narrator: “Nobody laughed. Somebody changed the subject, which is what people do when they have just heard something true.”
??? -  Female Scientist: “And still, you shun coffee. The lifeblood of late nights and early mornings.”
MC, amidst the dream, amused: “What can I say? Never felt the pull, especially with its penchant for wreaking havoc on electronics, right?”

Narrator: “Some evenings, the ones who stayed late ended up on the old couch in the corner, where the light from the screens did not quite reach. There was a woman beside you, more often than not, close enough that your shoulders touched.”
Narrator: “I could never quite remember her face. I remembered laughing, though. I had not done much of that since the war.”
???, with a burst of excitement: “Listen up, everyone! We've hit a milestone… the Temple of Time is real!”
MC: “The Temple of Time?”
???: “Precisely, newcomer. A relic granting passage through time, a marvel beyond the reach of automatons.”
MC: “Wait, really? That sounds great! We actually achieved something, we managed to make a discovery that truly is beyond machines.”
???: “Heh, you are still stuck on comparing humans to machines! Imbecile, we are above that! However, there’s a problem. Our colleague who managed to find it… died.”
Narrator: “The room went quiet. Beside you, the woman went very still.”

??? Female Scientist: “You two here are the ones whose brain waves are similar to his. From now on, you will join the experiment as Seekers. You will seek out this Temple of Time, carve the path to that place, and then report back to us.”
MC: “Another dream, and still no sign of Arielle. I’ll focus on the day ahead and plan during the weekend.
MC: “Huh? No dream this time around? And now it’s the weekend, I can do whatever I want.”
MC: “Still no sign of Arielle anywhere, I still don’t know what contract or covenant I got myself involved in.”

MC, a hint of mischief in his thoughts: "But this town isn’t all mysteries and covenants. There are some pretty interesting people here... especially the girls. Maybe it’s time for a different kind of exploring."
Narrator: “You did not get far with that plan. Your phone buzzed first.”

Viviane: “Good morning, my dear. Forgive an old woman her struggle with these modern contraptions; a lady such as myself has more interesting tales to tell. Yet it is not stories I bring you today, but a lead. There is something of great interest to you, head to the Military Branch HQ.”
MC: “Enlisting in the military? Again? It seems history does indeed love to repeat itself. And yet, my memories of the Automation War remain shrouded in fog. What secrets does my past future hold?”

Narrator: “And when you stepped outside, the town had gone quiet. No one at the bakery window, no carts on the road, not even the birds. Elysium had stopped the way a held breath stops, and every street seemed to lean the same way: toward the Military Branch.”
MC: "Hello, are you a member of the military?"
Guard: "Yes, can't you see these awesome muscles? this amazing helmet? and my big gun?"
MC, taken slightly aback: "Ah.. yes, how stupid of me to ask such a thing, but are you guys recruiting? I believe I'm interested in joining the military."
Guard, slightly irritated: "Oh great, another one.... yes, yes, we are still recruiting."
MC: "Excellent! What do I need to do to sign up?"
Guard: "First, we'll need to see if you can handle yourself. Follow me to the training area, and we'll put you through a basic combat drill."

Narrator: “The room was all maps and hard chairs, lit by a single lamp hanging low over the table, as if it were listening in. A grey morning pressed against the window, and beyond it the rooftops of Elysium went on with their quiet Saturday.”

Narrator: “The older man leaned on the table with both fists, as if the maps might try to leave without permission. A long midnight-blue coat, silver at the shoulders, grey coming in at his temples, and a silver star pinned over his heart. Across from him, a younger man with the same jaw and hair the color of embers leaned in too, one hand open, a gauntlet glowing soft blue on his forearm, trying very hard to be heard.”
Narrator: “Neither of them had noticed the door open. It was the kind of argument that had started long before today, and would not be finished today either.”
General Edward Blackwood: "Recruitment numbers are still below projections, Lohen. At this rate, our readiness could be compromised."
Lohen Blackwood: “Then stop hiding half of what we do from our own people! Nobody signs up to guard doors they’re never allowed to open. If we were honest with them, maybe...”
General Edward Blackwood, cutting him off: "Discipline does not need explanations. Our methods have stood the test of time."
Narrator: “Two pairs of blue eyes turned to the door at once.”
Narrator: “The younger one had been caught in the middle of a point he would now never finish, his hand still raised.”
Narrator: “The older one only straightened a little. He looked at you the way one looks at a point about to be proven.”
Guard: “Excuse me, General, I have brought a new volunteer who wishes to join us.”
Narrator: “The younger man’s face changed, and you found yourself wondering what exactly these two were to each other, and, more importantly, what they had been arguing about.”
General Edward Blackwood: "Ah, a potential recruit. You’re just in time to prove me right.”
General Edward Blackwood: “Name?"
MC: “I’m MC-NAME. What’s the argument about?”
General Edward Blackwood: “That information is confidential. However, if you manage to join us, you might just earn the right to learn more.”
General Edward Blackwood: “Lohen. Since you care so much about our recruits, you can test this one.”
Lohen Blackwood: “Yes sir.”
Lohen Blackwood: “Here, you'll face a couple of challenges to test your abilities. Do your best.”
MC, in a good mood: “Thanks”
Lohen Blackwood, impressed: “Not bad at all, that might even be a new record for the recruits.”
Lohen Blackwood, alarmed: "Damn, things were going too well! We have an emergency. Follow me, we need to evacuate immediately!”
Lohen Blackwood, surprised: “Is that… Natalie? Why isn’t she evacuating?”
Lohen Blackwood, surprised: “You know what MC, I have to take a detour, just keep moving forward and you’ll be out of here.”

Narrator: “Through the glass, far below, the warehouse floor had turned red. Caged lamps burned along the walls, and in their light a girl with a red ponytail sat cross-legged against the far wall, alone, eyes closed, hands resting open on her knees, as if the alarm were ringing for somebody else.”

Narrator: “The rest of the floor was moving. Shadows, dozens of them: things that walked like men and things that ran like wolves, something with far too many tails, something crawling along the wall behind the pillars. Every one of them was turned toward her.”
Narrator: “She was beautiful, and I could not look away from her, not even for a moment. She did not move and I could tell, this Natalie was in trouble, yet strangely still in control.”
MC, looking through the window, puzzled: "What are those?"
Lohen Blackwood, urging: "You don’t need to find out. It looks dangerous; just go!"
???, horrified: "Lohen, noooooooo!!!!"
MC, in awe: "Are these the shadows I saw?”
Narrator: “The warehouse was chaos. Red lamps stuttered along the walls, shots cracked off the concrete, and the floor between them was alive with shadows.”

Narrator: “At the edge of it all stood Lohen, helmet still on, smiling like a man in a pleasant dream. A woman made of shadow stood close in front of him, fox ears and a long ponytail, her dark fingers resting on his face as if she had every right to them. And behind him, her arms around his shoulders, was someone else: red hair, dark wings, and… a smile.”
